title: Neighbouring acetate participation
subtitle: An ester carbonyl oxygen pushes out tosylate: the acetoxonium ion

reactants.caption: trans-2-acetoxycyclohexyl tosylate + potassium acetate, in acetic acid
reactants.learnerPrompt: The tosylate leaves with help from the neighbouring ester. Draw that step.
hintTiers: Tosylate is a good leaving group, but a secondary cation is poor. Which atom of the neighbouring acetate group can reach round to the back of the C–OTs bond?
The carbonyl oxygen of the ester attacks the carbon carrying tosylate, from the side opposite the leaving group, and the C–O bond to tosylate breaks. Two arrows: a five-membered ring forms.
Lone pair of the ester C=O oxygen → new bond to the carbon carrying tosylate; that C–O bond → a lone pair on the tosylate oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Acetate could attack from outside, but that SN2 would invert the carbon and give the cis diacetate. The product is the trans diacetate, and the trans tosylate reacts hundreds of times faster than the cis one: the neighbouring ester takes part.
The oxygen bonded to the ring would make a strained three-membered ring. The carbonyl oxygen can reach round and make a five-membered ring instead, a much easier ring to form.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right that tosylate leaves, but a bare secondary cation is not what forms here. Which neighbouring oxygen pushes it out from behind?

acetoxonium-ion.caption: the acetoxonium ion (a 1,3-dioxolan-2-ylium ion) + tosylate + acetate
hintTiers: The positive charge is shared by both oxygens and the carbon between them. Acetate attacks a ring carbon from behind, as in an SN2 reaction. Which bond breaks?
Acetate bonds to one of the two ring carbons; the C–O bond to that carbon breaks, and its pair makes a C=O bond, while the other C=O⁺ pair goes back to its oxygen. Three arrows.
Acetate oxygen lone pair → new bond to a ring CH; that carbon's C–O bond → a C=O π bond to the central carbon; the C=O⁺ π bond → a lone pair on the other oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Attack at the central carbon is possible (with water it gives the cis hydroxy acetate, as in the Woodward modification of the Prévost reaction), but in acetic acid, acetate opens the ring at a ring carbon and gives the trans diacetate.
Tosylate is a very weak nucleophile and its return just goes back to the start. Acetate opens the ring.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right bonds, but that leaves a negative and a positive oxygen on the same ester. Push the negative oxygen's lone pair into a C=O bond and move the C=O⁺ pair back to its oxygen.

steps.explanationAfterStep: The carbonyl oxygen of the neighbouring ester displaces tosylate from behind, giving a five-membered acetoxonium ion. This needs the two groups anti to each other on the ring (both axial): it is an intramolecular SN2, with inversion at that carbon. The app does not check stereochemistry yet.

Acetate opens the ring by a second SN2 reaction at a ring carbon, again with inversion. Two inversions make retention overall: the trans tosylate gives the trans diacetate. Starting from a single enantiomer, the product is racemic, because the acetoxonium ion has a mirror plane and either ring carbon can be attacked.

mechanismSummary: In trans-2-acetoxycyclohexyl tosylate the ester carbonyl oxygen sits anti to the leaving group. It displaces tosylate from behind (inversion), giving a five-membered acetoxonium ion in which the positive charge is shared by two oxygens. Acetate then opens the ring at a ring carbon (a second inversion). Two inversions give retention: the product is trans-1,2-diacetoxycyclohexane. The cis tosylate cannot do this and reacts hundreds of times more slowly (Winstein). The app does not check stereochemistry yet.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 36
